title: UFOs: A Very Efficient Multivariate Public Key Signature Scheme
abstract: We present UFOs, a multivariate public-key signature scheme in the Unbalanced Oil and Vinegar (UOV) family. The scheme replaces generic quadratic polynomials with a structured subclass based on Frobenius-type quadratic forms, yielding a compressed public-key representation while retaining the efficient UOV signing procedure. We describe the key-generation, signing, and verification algorithms, and we detail the derivation of the public system from a compact secret description. We discuss security in the standard multivariate setting, including direct algebraic attacks and key-recovery approaches, and we formalize the underlying computational problems induced by the proposed structure. Finally, we report implementation results quantifying the costs of key generation, signing, and verification, as well as the resulting public-key and signature sizes.

1    Introduction

Modern digital infrastructures rely on digital signatures; post-quantum designs
based on multivariate polynomial systems remain attractive due to fast verification
and conservative hardness assumptions. A canonical representative is Unbalanced
Oil and Vinegar (UOV) [34], where signing inverts a structured MQ map using
an oil–vinegar trapdoor.

Contributions. We introduce UFOs (Unbalanced Frobenius Oil and Vinegar with
Schedule), a UOV-type signature scheme whose public key is specified by a small
                                                                           a   b
number of Frobenius blocks over Fq , i.e., sparse sums of monomials xp y p . This
reduces public-key size while preserving the standard UOV signing procedure
(vinegar sampling followed by an Fp -linear solve in the oil variables).
    This version updates [24] in light of the exponent-only attack of [2] by formal-
izing schedule-selection criteria and instantiating hardened exponent schedules.
    We provide (i) a complete specification, (ii) a concrete security analysis against
the main known attack families, and (iii) parameter sets with proof-of-concept
performance measurements.
Technical overview. The scheme works over an odd-characteristic base field and
an extension Fq = Fpe , and uses homogeneous public maps. After descent to
Fp , verification remains evaluation of an MQ system, while signing reduces to
solving an oe × me linear system over Fp (square when m = o). The main design
parameter beyond (o, v, m, p, e) is the exponent schedule {(ak , bk )}ℓk=1 ⊂ (Z/eZ)2 ,
which governs the resistance to direct low-dimensional algebraic models.

2.5    UOV scheme and its trapdoor
We now give a short overview of the UOV scheme; we refer to the specification
document [34] for full details.
     UOV is a trapdoor construction for multivariate quadratic (MQ) systems. It
starts from a “central” quadratic map F = (F1 , . . . , Fm ) : Fn → Fm in variables
(x1 , . . . , xn ), with n = v + m split into v “vinegar” variables and m “oil” variables.
The defining property is that F contains no oil–oil quadratic terms: once the
vinegar variables are fixed, each Fr becomes an affine function of the oil variables.
     The public key is the disguised system Pub = F ◦ S, where S : Fn → Fn
is a secret invertible affine transformation. Given a target h ∈ Fm , inverting
Pub(x) = h without the secret is assumed hard.
     To use the trapdoor, one first chooses random values for the vinegar variables,
then solves the resulting linear system in the oil variables to obtain u such that
F (u) = h. Finally, one outputs x = S −1 (u), which satisfies Pub(x) = h by
construction.


3     Design Rationale
Main design idea The objective is to preserve the UOV trapdoor paradigm
while enabling a compact public-key representation. Inspired by recent structured
MQ signature proposals (e.g., SNOVA, QR-UOV, MAYO), the public map is


                                            4
constrained to a family that can be generated from a small amount of randomness.
Note that in an information-theoretic sense such keys are not distributed like
fully random MQ instances: key generation produces (typically overdetermined)
systems with a guaranteed hidden solution (the oil space). The relevant question
is whether this structural bias yields an efficient distinguisher or can be turned
into practical key-recovery/forgery attacks. However, if such a distinguisher could
be constructed, it could be transformed into a procedure that distinguishes
between univariate polynomials that possess roots and those that do not. This
appears highly implausible, given that (for several natural input models) the
general problem of determining the existence of a root is NP-hard [5].
    Shrinking multivariate public keys has been a central theme in recent propos-
als [25], including MAYO [4], QR-UOV [18], and SNOVA [23]. We work with homo-
geneous equations over an odd-characteristic base field. This avoids characteristic-
two subtleties, where the Frobenius map is F2 -linear and quadratic/bilinear
representations behave differently [22,13]. More generally, both the base-field
characteristic and the choice between homogeneous and affine public maps affect
design and cryptanalysis [35,11].

Design principle: evaluate residual triplets. This motivates a schedule-selection
methodology based on the ten possible residual triplets, obtained by canceling any
two out of the five blocks. For each residual triplet, we evaluate two complementary
quantities.
    First, we consider the univariate span L: this is the length of the smallest
cyclic interval containing the six residual endpoints. A large value of L means
that no common Frobenius shift can compress the triplet into a short univariate
window.
    Second, we consider the best two-anchor bivariate model. For every choice of
shift σ, orientations, and anchors (r, s), we compute the two bidegrees induced
by the residual indices and derive the corresponding resultant-based score. The
attacker will of course choose the most favorable such representation, so the
relevant defensive quantity is the minimum score over all these choices; good
schedules maximize this minimum.

Geometric interpretation. These criteria admit a simple geometric interpretation
on the cycle Z/eZ. Each block contributes an ordered pair of endpoints (ak , bk ),
and after two cancellations the attacker sees three such pairs, i.e., six marked
points on the cycle.
    The univariate criterion asks whether these six points fit inside one short arc.
If they do, then one obtains a low-degree one-variable description.
    The bivariate criterion asks whether the same six points can be organized
around two centers (the anchors r and s), after possibly flipping the orientation


                                          9
of each surviving pair and comparing the original triplet with a shifted copy. If
the endpoints assigned to the X-side stay close to one anchor and those assigned
to the Y -side stay close to the other, then the two equations have small bidegrees,
which leads to a low-degree resultant attack. Thus, from a geometric viewpoint, a
good exponent schedule is one for which every residual triplet is simultaneously:
 – spread out enough to resist short-arc univariate compression, and
 – misaligned enough to resist concentration around two anchors.

Practical guideline for choosing exponent pairs. In practice, this suggests the
following rules. One should avoid schedules for which:
 1. some two-block cancellation leaves six endpoints contained in a short cyclic
    interval;
 2. some residual triplet can be partitioned, after orientation choices and a
    Frobenius shift, into two small neighborhoods around two anchors;
 3. several differences bk − ak mod e are repeated or nearly repeated up to sign,
    which tends to create aligned residual configurations.
Conversely, good schedules are obtained by maximizing, over all residual triplets,
the worst-case univariate span and the worst-case bivariate score. This provides
a concrete and reproducible exponent-selection strategy that is fully compatible
with the original F-UOV format and algorithms, while explicitly targeting the
direct algebraic attack surface created by the Frobenius index pattern.

Additional exponent-schedule diagnostics. Beyond the basic univariate-span and
two-anchor bivariate tests, the exponent schedule can be screened through sev-
eral further diagnostics of the type studied in [2]. These diagnostics are not
security proofs, but they help identify schedules that create especially simple
low-dimensional algebraic models after cancelling some Frobenius blocks.
    A first family of diagnostics concerns affine restrictions. If one fixes a direction
U ∈ Fnq and evaluates the public map on an affine line V +xU , then after cancelling
two blocks the remaining expression contains both quadratic Frobenius terms
and linear Frobenius terms in x. In this setting, a useful question is whether
the residual exponents can be covered by a small number of anchors on the
cyclic index set Z/eZ, with small maximal distance to an anchor. Small covering
radii indicate that the affine restriction may admit a compact few-variable
representation. Hence one diagnostic is to measure, for the residual indices, the
best two-, three-, or four-anchor covering radius.
    A second family concerns common zeros of several public blocks. If one searches

D.4    Direct algebraic effect: densification of each public block
This densification is the main reason why such an output layer may be relevant
from a cryptanalytic viewpoint. In the original design, a public block is exposed
through a single exponent pair (ak , bk ). Even though the full public map is a
sum of several blocks, each component remains individually sparse and therefore
potentially accessible to attacks that attempt to isolate a few blocks, cancel some
of them, and exploit the low-dimensional structure of the residual equation.
    After composition with Tk , the public contribution of the k-th block is no
longer attached to a single visible pair, but to the full collection

    First, a single block can no longer be read as a single bilinear relation between
two visible Frobenius layers. Instead, it simultaneously contributes to many such
layer interactions. This makes the direct identification of a residual equation with
a very small number of exponent pairs less transparent.
    Second, attacks based on restricting the public map to a public line and
then trying to derive a very small univariate or bivariate model become less
natural. Indeed, the direct resultant attack of [2] crucially exploits the fact that
after cancelling two blocks, the remaining three terms still correspond to a very
sparse visible exponent pattern admitting two compatible low-degree bivariate
rewritings. If each residual block has first been mixed with all its Frobenius shifts,
the attacker no longer sees one term per block in that sense, but rather a denser
superposition whose elimination profile is much less obvious.
    Third, the various orbit-style diagnostics discussed in [2] become harder to
interpret directly at the level of visible blocks. Those diagnostics are driven by
the placement of a small number of explicit endpoints or layer differences. Public
output mixing does not destroy the underlying Frobenius symmetries, but it
spreads each block over its full orbit at the output level, so that the naive visible
endpoint schedule is no longer the relevant one for direct algebraic modeling.

D.6    Possible implementation choices

Several implementation choices are possible for the maps Tk .
    A first possibility is to sample a fully dense Fp -linear map, i.e., to use all
coefficients tk,i . This gives maximal output spreading, but also increases the cost
of evaluating the public map.
    A second possibility is to restrict each Tk to a sparse linearized polynomial, for
instance with only a few nonzero coefficients. This already destroys the one-pair
visibility of a block while keeping evaluation costs lower.
    A third possibility is to require Tk to be invertible as an Fp -linear map. This
is not necessary for correctness, since signing and verification only require public
evaluation, but invertibility may be desirable if one wants to avoid collapsing
too much information at the output level or introducing trivial rank defects. In
practice, invertibility can be tested during parameter generation, or enforced by
deriving Tk from a public seed until a suitable map is obtained.

D.7   Security interpretation

From the viewpoint of the two analyses considered in this work, the expected
effect of public output mixing is favorable. The first part of this work emphasizes
the role of sparse Frobenius representations in obtaining compact public keys and
discusses direct algebraic attacks through line restrictions and common isotropic
subspaces. The second part shows that for the published exponent schedule, a
particularly small residual three-term equation admits a low-degree bivariate
elimination attack. Both perspectives rely, in one form or another, on the fact
that the public blocks remain individually sparse and directly visible.
    The proposed output layer acts precisely on this point: it keeps the hidden
oil space and the signing mechanism intact, but it makes each visible block much
less elementary. Heuristically, this should increase the difficulty of:

 – isolating a very small number of residual visible blocks after cancellation;
 – recognizing a low-degree bivariate rewriting tied to a specific exponent sched-
   ule;
 – constructing very small orbit-style or layer-based direct models from the
   public block decomposition alone.

   In that sense, public output mixing appears to be a plausible hardening option
against the currently known direct attacks.


D.8   Limitations and caveats

At the same time, this should not be overstated. The argument above is structural
and heuristic, not a proof of increased security.
    First, the mixed scheme still has strong Frobenius symmetries. The maps
Tk are themselves linearized polynomials, so they do not remove the semilinear
nature of the construction; they only make it less sparse at the visible output
level.
    Second, public output mixing may introduce new dependencies. For exam-
ple, if some Tk have low rank or interact in a special way with the original
blocks, one might obtain unexpected linear relations among coordinates of the
public map. These would have to be excluded by parameter design or analyzed
cryptanalytically.
    Third, while the current resultant-style attack seems to rely on visible block
sparsity, it is conceivable that more global multivariable or orbit-based attacks
could be adapted to the mixed setting. In particular, once all Frobenius shifts of
a block are made public simultaneously, new elimination strategies may become
available at a different level of abstraction.
    For these reasons, the present proposal should be viewed as a possible hard-
ening direction rather than as a validated repair.

E     Conclusions
We proposed UFOs, a multivariate signature scheme that combines a UOV-style
trapdoor with public equations restricted to sparse sums of Frobenius forms,
leading to compact keys.
    For our Level I parameter set, the public key consists of 5 × 61 field elements
in F31 together with a short seed, totaling about 1600 bits (roughly 206 bytes).
Signatures follow a hash-and-sign paradigm. Signing mainly requires arithmetic
in F31 and inversion of a 61 × 61 linear system. Verification is performed over
an extension of F31 and involves only a small number of multiplications. Each
signature contains 5 × 61 field elements (about 1600 bits) plus a 256-bit salt, i.e.,
under 250 bytes.
    At these parameters, public keys and signatures are competitive in size with
widely deployed schemes and leading post-quantum candidates, while keeping
operations simple.
    From a security standpoint, the construction retains the UOV trapdoor struc-
ture and reduces the main attack avenues to either (i) recovering an equivalent
oil subspace from the embedded isotropy constraints, or (ii) solving the resulting
sparse Frobenius MQ systems over Fq (or, after expansion, quadratic systems over
Fp ). We provide concrete cost estimates for these attacks in the corresponding
models.
    Several directions remain open, including:
 – a tighter analysis of the embedded-constraint systems, particularly in the
   setting where the public “known part” (i.e. the matrices A∗ ) is fixed once
   and for all, possibly sparse,
 – optimized, constant-time, leakage-resilient implementations,
 – extensions such as threshold variants of UFOs.
